references.label: JPAC FFP LD storage
references.citation: JPAC. Guidelines for the Blood Transfusion Services: 7.5.1 Fresh Frozen Plasma, Leucocyte Depleted, section 7.5.1.3 Storage. Last updated 17 February 2026; accessed 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt:
The component should be stored at a core temperature of -25°C or below for a maximum of 36 months.
For indications other than unexpected major haemorrhage, the component should be used within 24 hours of thawing.
references.reviewNote: Component-specific storage, not dose validation. Refrigerated 120-hour maximum requires the indication-specific, validated temperature/thawing procedure; labile factors decline. No refreezing.

references.label: JPAC cryoprecipitate LD storage
references.citation: JPAC. Guidelines for the Blood Transfusion Services: 7.5.3 Cryoprecipitate, Leucocyte Depleted, section 7.5.3.3 Storage. Last updated 17 February 2026; accessed 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt: Once thawed, the component must not be refrozen and should be used immediately. If delay is unavoidable, the component should be stored at ambient temperature and used within 4 hours.
references.reviewNote: Standard single-unit component: maximum 36 months frozen at −25°C or colder; not the provisional extended post-thaw product.

references.label: JPAC pooled cryoprecipitate LD storage
references.citation: JPAC. Guidelines for the Blood Transfusion Services: 7.5.4 Cryoprecipitate, Pooled, Leucocyte Depleted, section 7.5.4.3 Storage. Last updated 17 February 2026; accessed 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt: Once thawed, the component must not be refrozen and should be transfused as soon as possible. If delay is unavoidable, the component should be stored at ambient temperature and used within 4 hours.
references.reviewNote: Ordinary pooled component: maximum 36 months frozen at −25°C or colder; no universal 120-hour post-thaw instruction.

references.label: JPAC provisional extended cryoprecipitate
references.citation: JPAC. Guidelines for the Blood Transfusion Services: Annex 3 A3.9 Cryoprecipitate, Pooled, Leucocyte Depleted, Extended Shelf-life Post-thaw, section A3.9.3 Storage. Provisional component; last updated 17 February 2026; accessed 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt:
Extended Shelf-life Post-thaw cryoprecipitate may be stored up to 120 hours at 4 ±2°C following thawing.
Once re-warmed, Extended Shelf-life Post-thaw cryoprecipitate should not be placed back in the refrigerator.
references.reviewNote: Separately labelled provisional component only; validated thawing, rewarming at 33–37°C until visible precipitate dissolves (maximum 20 minutes), and issue/return rules apply. Not ordinary cryoprecipitate or whole-component certification.

references.label: PROPPR 2015 protocol
references.citation: PROPPR Study Group. Pragmatic Randomized Optimal Platelet and Plasma Ratios: complete study protocol. Component delivery and Table 4, pp. 22–23. Opened 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt: 1 platelet dose equal to either 6 random-donor units or 1 apheresis unit
references.reviewNote: Trial-specific platelet-unit equivalence; not one adult platelet dose per RBC unit or a universal MHP pack.

references.label: PROPPR 2015 outcomes
references.citation: Holcomb JB, Tilley BC, Baraniuk S, et al. Transfusion of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells in a 1:1:1 vs a 1:1:2 ratio and mortality in patients with severe trauma: the PROPPR randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015;313(5):471–482. doi:10.1001/jama.2015.12.
references.reviewNote: Full results opened 1 November 2026: no statistically significant 24-hour/30-day all-cause mortality difference; more haemostasis and fewer exsanguination deaths, but time to haemostasis among achievers was not significantly different.

references.label: NICE NG39 major haemorrhage
references.citation: NICE. Major trauma: assessment and initial management (NG39). Recommendations 1.5.13–1.5.14, 1.5.21, 1.5.24 and 1.5.27. Current official recommendations opened 1 November 2026.
references.excerpt: Use physiological criteria that include the patient's haemodynamic status and their response to immediate volume resuscitation to activate the major haemorrhage protocol.
references.reviewNote: Adult trauma initial plasma:RBC 1:1, early laboratory-guided treatment and dominant-TBI cerebral-perfusion exception; not a universal regimen for other bleeding causes.

references.label: NICE NG232 selected head injury TXA
references.citation: NICE. Head injury: assessment and early management (NG232). Recommendation 1.3.17 [2023]. Current official recommendations opened 1 November 2026.
references.reviewNote: Consider, not universal: head injury GCS ≤12, no suspected active extracranial bleeding; age ≥16, 2 g IV bolus as soon as possible within 2 hours, before imaging. Separate from bleeding-trauma regimen; off-label use noted by NICE.

references.label: Rossaint 2023 calcium
references.citation: Rossaint R, Afshari A, Bouillon B, et al. European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition. Crit Care. 2023;27:80. Recommendation 31 and rationale. doi:10.1186/s13054-023-04327-7.
references.excerpt: We recommend that ionised calcium levels be monitored and maintained within the normal range following major trauma and especially during massive transfusion (Grade 1C).
references.reviewNote: Normal range approximately 1.1–1.3 mmol/L, pH-dependent. Not an automatic calcium dose per RBC pack; full primary guideline opened 1 November 2026.

references.label: Rossaint 2023 BP target
references.citation: Rossaint R, et al. European trauma guideline: sixth edition. Crit Care. 2023;27:80. Recommendation 13 and rationale. doi:10.1186/s13054-023-04327-7.
references.reviewNote: Initial adult traumatic haemorrhage SBP 80–90 mmHg pending bleeding control, without brain/spinal injury; TBI/spinal injury require CNS perfusion protection. Full primary guideline opened 1 November 2026.

references.label: NICE NG24 thresholds
references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Blood transfusion (NG24), recommendations 1.5.2–1.5.3. Published 2015; last updated 26 February 2026.
references.excerpt: 1.5.2 When using a restrictive red blood cell transfusion threshold, consider a threshold of 70 g/litre and a haemoglobin concentration target of 70 to 90 g/litre after transfusion. [2015] 1.5.3 Consider a red blood cell transfusion threshold of 80 g/litre and a haemoglobin concentration target of 80 to 100 g/litre after transfusion for people with acute coronary syndrome.

references.label: MINT 2023 result
references.citation: Carson JL, Brooks MM, Hébert PC, et al. Restrictive or liberal transfusion strategy in myocardial infarction and anemia. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(26):2446-2456.
references.excerpt: In patients with acute myocardial infarction and anemia, a liberal transfusion strategy did not significantly reduce the risk of recurrent myocardial infarction or death at 30 days. However, potential harms of a restrictive transfusion strategy cannot be excluded.

references.label: TRAIN 2024 result

references.label: HEMOTION 2024

references.label: BSH DOAC Bleeding 2023

cards.question: What ratios are used in major haemorrhage protocols?
cards.answer: PROPPR 2015 used plasma:platelet-equivalents:RBC 1:1:1 in severe trauma: 6 plasma units, 1 adult platelet dose (about 6 whole-blood-derived platelet units or 1 apheresis unit), and 6 RBC units, not one adult platelet dose per RBC. More achieved haemostasis and fewer died from exsanguination; 24-hour/30-day mortality differences were not statistically significant. NICE NG39 initial adult major-trauma plasma:RBC is 1:1; follow the local MHP and transition promptly to laboratory/viscoelastic-guided treatment. Activation uses physiology, bleeding and response, not predicted units alone. Measure ionised calcium frequently and replace by protocol to the normal range (approximately 1.1–1.3 mmol/L; laboratory/pH context). Ratios and targets are not universal across bleeding causes.

cards.question: When is prothrombin complex concentrate preferred over FFP?
cards.answer: For warfarin reversal in major bleeding (25–50 U/kg with vitamin K, BSH 2018), or factor replacement in liver disease where volume load from FFP is harmful; PCC restores INR within minutes versus hours for FFP.

cards.question: How is ROTEM/TEG used to guide blood product use?
cards.answer: FIBTEM A5 <12 mm → fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate; EXTEM CT >80 s → FFP or PCC; EXTEM A5 <40 mm with normal FIBTEM → platelets; ML >15% → tranexamic acid (ITACTIC trial).
